claims.text: Degradation of Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 during elevated-temperature gas exposure is governed by competition between a protective multilayer oxide scale and internal degradation involving segregation and subsurface phase reactions.
Under oxidizing conditions, synergistic interactions among Cr, Ti, and minor Al rapidly produce a protective oxide scale in the target alloy.
The oxide scale formed under oxidizing conditions is thin and adherent and protects the underlying fcc matrix.
Reducing conditions suppress protective-scale formation and thereby cause internal oxidation and phase-boundary degradation.
The as-printed target alloy has a stable fcc matrix.
The as-printed target alloy contains minimal pre-existing precipitates and internal oxidation.
The proposed test exposes samples at 700–900 °C under systematically varied O2:H2 ratios for up to 100 hours.
The proposed test compares the as-printed alloy with a homogenized, annealed version.
The relevant structural mediator is the continuity and composition of a multilayer scale containing a Cr-rich layer and possibly an Al- or Ti-modified sublayer.
Subsurface elemental segregation or phase transformations can arise at the matrix/oxide interface.
A continuous oxide scale limits further oxygen ingress and preserves fcc-matrix integrity.
Lower O2:H2 ratios will produce a thicker, more porous, or more discontinuous oxide scale than predominantly oxidizing atmospheres.
Reducing exposures will produce more internal oxidation or deleterious phase-boundary reactions than oxidizing exposures.
Predominantly oxidizing exposures will better preserve mechanical integrity than reducing exposures.
Before exposure, the as-printed baseline has limited oxide formation and no significant internal degradation.
Processing history and microstructural heterogeneity may alter oxidation and degradation outcomes.
The transition gas ratio and the individual contributions of Cr, Ti, and Al are not quantitatively specified.
The mechanism is falsified if changing O2:H2 ratio produces no systematic differences in scale quality, subsurface phases, or mechanical performance.
